headline: Hong Kong gave Joshua Wong 10 more years.
summary: A Hong Kong court sentenced Joshua Wong to 10 more years on Thursday for colluding with foreign forces under the national security law. He pleaded guilty in September to lobbying for sanctions against Beijing in 2020, with Nathan Law. Wong is 30, has spent six years in jail and was due out in January. Human Rights Watch called it cruel.

cover_question.q: Is asking for sanctions a crime?

cover_answer: In Hong Kong since 2020, yes. Ten years' worth.
table_question: Should asking outsiders for help ever be a crime?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Hong Kong, a man named Joshua Wong was sent to jail for ten more years. He didn't hurt anyone. He asked other countries to push back on his government, and Hong Kong made that a crime. He started speaking up as a schoolboy, about the price of lunch. Ten years is longer than you've been alive. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: School lunches they know. Ten years against their own age is a length they can feel.
5-7.why_long: A child this age takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the one that fits: a schoolboy who spoke up about the price of lunch, and ten years measured against their own age. The law's name and the word collusion stay off the card. Expect "will he get out?" Yes, but not for a long time.

8-12.script: Joshua Wong started a student group in Hong Kong at 14. A year later 100,000 people marched with it, and the government backed down. In 2020 a new law made asking abroad for sanctions a crime. Wong did, pleaded guilty, and got ten years on top of six. The rule changed. He kept playing.
8-12.why: A rule in one line, a kid who won once, years they can add up.
8-12.why_long: This age is checking rules and whether they are fair, so the script states the rule in one line, asking other countries for sanctions is collusion, and lets them add the years: ten on top of six. The anchor is a 14-year-old whose group made a government back down. Expect "why didn't he leave like his friend?" The BBC doesn't say.

13-17.script: Wong asked foreign governments to sanction Beijing in 2020. Hong Kong's law calls that collusion, and he pleaded guilty. If a law can make a petition a crime, what does guilty mean? Second: Nathan Law did the same and left for the UK. Wong stayed. Which one did more for Hong Kong?
13-17.why: Two true things: he broke the law as written, and the law was written to catch him. They can hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: Wong broke the law as written, and the law was written in 2020 to catch exactly what he did. The script hands them both, then the choice Law and Wong made differently, leave or stay. Expect "would you have stayed?" Answer it straight; they are testing whether you will argue honestly.

5-7.a: In 2020 Hong Kong made asking other countries for help a crime.

8-12.a: He asked other countries to punish Beijing. That's the crime.

8-12.q: Was he a kid when he began?
8-12.a: He was 14. A year later 100,000 people marched with him.

13-17.q: Is asking for sanctions a crime?
13-17.a: Since 2020 in Hong Kong, yes. He pleaded guilty. Ten years.

13-17.q: Why did he stay when Law left?
13-17.a: The BBC doesn't say. He stayed, ran for office, and was barred.
